extracted.intended_audience: general readers; historians and researchers of British humour, satire, and periodical culture; cartoonists and illustrators
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of Punch (or The London Charivari), describing its founding, editorial stance, contributors, artistry, influence, circulation, and later revivals and closure. Useful as a reference on the magazine's historical role in British humour and cartooning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of the contemporary, social, and political scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch published satire of the contemporary, social, and political scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents this topical satirical focus as a core defining characteristic of Punch and the primary content domain it engaged — an intended criterion for what counted as Punch's subject-matter and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophisticated humour and absence of offensive material
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch became a staple for British drawing rooms because of its sophisticated humour and absence of offensive material, especially when viewed against the satirical press of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece frames 'sophistication' and avoiding overtly offensive content as qualities that contributed to Punch's respectability and audience reach; this can be read as a standard for the magazine's tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and development of political cartoons ('cartoon' terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch helped coin the term 'cartoon' in its modern sense (first used in Punch in 1843) and appropriated the term to refer to its political cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises the centrality of cartoons to the magazine's identity and influence; implies that strong, topical cartooning was a key quality metric for Punch-style satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistry and roster of notable illustrators (the 'Punch Brotherhood')
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch published work by prominent artists (e.g., John Leech, John Tenniel, Charles Keene) and this group became known as 'The Punch Brotherhood'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights high-quality, named illustrators as essential to Punch's reputation; presence of distinguished cartoonists/illustrators is presented as a marker of the magazine's artistic standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions by eminent authors and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch featured contributions from many notable writers and editors (e.g., Charles Dickens, Thackeray, W. C. Sellar, P. G. Wodehouse) and listed a long roster of editors and authors across its run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing of prominent literary contributors is used to indicate editorial quality and cultural status; inclusion of recognized literary figures functioned as a quality criterion for the magazine's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation, popularity, and longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch's circulation grew from 40,000 copies a week by 1850 to over 100,000 by 1910, peaking in the 1940s; it was published (with interruptions) from 1841 until final closure in 2002.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats sustained high circulation, wide readership, and long publication lifespan as measures of Punch's success and cultural impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and international emulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch was widely emulated worldwide and inspired numerous 'Punch' periodicals across the British Empire and beyond (e.g., Japan Punch, China Punch, Melbourne Punch, Punch in Canada).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International imitation and the magazine's role in inspiring other publications are presented as evidence of its influence — a criterion for assessing cultural reach and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding and mascot (use of Mr Punch / visual identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The editors took the anarchic puppet Mr Punch as their mascot; the character appears on many covers and inspired the magazine's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent visual branding (mascot/masthead) is described as part of Punch's identity and recognisability, implying that strong branding contributed to its success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practices and institutional relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch's relationships with printers/publishers (Bradbury and Evans), other papers (The Times), and intellectual journals (Westminster Review) helped grant it respectability and market placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article indicates that publishing partnerships, editorial networks, and institutional affiliations were important to the magazine's distribution and reputation — operational criteria affecting cultural standing.
